alloc_table.note: Allocating and freeing a table against a live population of three thousand composite objects. `roadmap.md` M4 named this benchmark and `malloc.c` pointed at it in a comment for as long as it did not exist - that its linear scan and its 32-byte header were unfixed "because nothing has measured them". 28138.160 on the first-fit allocator, 355.731 on the segregated-fit one that replaced it: 79x, and it is the scan rather than anything clever. The old malloc walked one list holding every block, free *or allocated*, so an allocation cost what the heap already contained. **The live population is what makes this number mean anything** - on an empty heap both allocators look the same, which is how this went unmeasured for so long. Includes the collector, which cannot be separated out and does not need to be: under -icount its share is identical between two runs. **355.731 -> 288.870 (-18.8%), recorded on 2 October and attributed by building the benchmark either side of 3b52773**: 291.9 both before and after the libc's word-at-a-time memory functions, so all of it is the allocator finding a bin by its bit (ecf6957, 30 September, `testing.md` 18.307, which measured -17.8% then and did not raise this baseline).
alloc_table.unit: counter ticks per operation, QEMU -icount shift=0

context_switch.note: One of the three that touch no Lua. Two changes moved it in opposite directions and the net is what matters: 9.812 -> 6.875 when the FP register file stopped being saved on every switch, then 6.875 -> 8.375 when round robin became a priority queue. Net -14.6% against the eager-FP round-robin number, with priorities and preemption-on-wake gained. The +21.8% half is the cost of indexing eight queues and maintaining an occupancy mask instead of following one head pointer; the obvious version, which scanned the levels, cost twice that and the benchmark caught it the same day. **8.375 -> 12.066 (+44%), and it is the SMP programme rather than one change.** Measured on 19 September 2026 by building the benchmark at the commit that recorded 8.375 (802d0be, 5 September) and at the last commit before that evening's work: 8.625 there, 12.064 here - so the growth is everything between, which is per-core runqueues with a lock each, a lock on every pool, the preemption path and the IPI. Nobody re-measured for two weeks because `make test` does not run the benchmarks; `roadmap.md` has finding where it went, by bisecting these two numbers. That evening's own work - capabilities moving to the process - cost 12.064 -> 12.066, which is nothing. **12.066 -> 12.316 (+2.1%) for a thread's own pointer** (`threads.md` step 2): one comparison of the two threads' records and a register written only when they differ, so a switch between kernel threads writes nothing. Three versions were measured before this one was kept - saving and restoring on every switch cost 3.6%, and saving only when a user pointer was loaded cost 4.1%, the branch and the per-CPU lookup being dearer than the register read. Under -icount this is two loads and a not-taken branch counted at full price; on a real processor a predicted branch is close to free. **12.316 -> 13.441 by 2 October, then 13.441 -> 12.754 the same day** (`testing.md` 18.343). What stays above 12.316 is on purpose and attributed by `make bench-profile` at 42f0e71 against now, 193 instructions a switch against 205: the per-core time Monitor shows (de73ffb, 24 September - two comparisons with the idle thread a switch) and a choice clearing the preemption a wake asked for (18.340). The same day's lock and per-core work took back 0.7 of the 1.1 ticks.
context_switch.unit: counter ticks per operation, QEMU -icount shift=0

exception.note: The cost of taking and returning from a synchronous exception. 7.250 -> 7.562, +4.3%, and it is the price of lazy FP save rather than a regression to chase: every exception now begins by asking whether it is an FP trap, because that question has to be answered before anything else looks at the frame. One comparison, paid on every exception, to save the whole register file on every context switch - `context_switch` went down 29.9% and `ipc_roundtrip` 16.2% in the same change.
exception.unit: counter ticks per operation, QEMU -icount shift=0

gc_pause_max.note: The worst single collector step, measured in a process. 78221, drifting up with what the process carries in the same way serialize does and by far less: 78129 before gfx, 78199 after, 78221 with the font. A long step is dominated by the 3000-object heap the benchmark builds rather than by a handful of library tables. Before that it was 77860, running inside the kernel with interrupts masked. Leaving EL1 cost the interpreter +0.3% and nothing else: a collector step costs the same at either privilege level. Interrupts are live in the window now, because a process cannot mask them, and for a pause metric that is more honest rather than less - a pause the user feels includes the tick that landed in it. 78371 -> 78746 (+0.5%, inside the tolerance) recorded with the rest on 2 October.
gc_pause_max.unit: counter ticks per operation, QEMU -icount shift=0

ipc_roundtrip.note: A minimal message: the floor of the IPC path, including the capability lookup. 36.251 -> 30.376 from lazy FP save, then back to 36.438 with the priority scheduler - a round trip is two switches, so it pays the policy twice. Net flat against two days earlier, which is the honest way to read it: lazy FP bought the priority queue rather than the priority queue being free. What was gained for it is a bounded wait for a higher-priority thread, which this benchmark cannot see. **36.438 -> 62.960 (+73%), of which 1.6% is the capability table moving to the process and the rest is the SMP programme.** Measured on 19 September 2026: 37.629 at the commit that recorded 36.438, 61.944 at the last commit before that evening, 62.960 after it. The evening's 1.6% is one indirection and an acquire load on every resolve, which is what a table shared by a process's threads costs; putting the table's lock on the read path cost 10% instead, which is why readers do not take it (`design.md` 4.3). The 70% before it is per-core runqueues, locks in every pool and endpoint, and the IPI - and `roadmap.md` carries finding out which, by bisecting. Then 62.960 -> 63.523 (+0.9%) for the same thread pointer, which a round trip pays twice because it is two switches. **63.523 -> 68.088 over the fortnight after, then 68.088 -> 59.397 (-12.8%) on 2 October** (`testing.md` 18.343), taken apart instruction by instruction with `make bench-profile` against the kernel of 5 September: 1090 instructions a round trip against 603. The seven locks are four processors' price and stay; what had grown around each went - `panicking` and `this_cpu` and `thread_current` calls made inline, the lock's wait moved out of line so a free lock costs one try, messages with no data copying nothing, and the switch and the block reading the per-core register once. 951 instructions now.
ipc_roundtrip.unit: counter ticks per operation, QEMU -icount shift=0

serialize.note: Best of five processes within a run. **This benchmark is sensitive to what else is in the process**, not only to the serialiser: every library the image opens is more objects for the collector to pace against. 1450.574 -> 1498.325, +3.3%, when the PDF scanner and the inflate kit joined the user image; `serialize.c` was untouched. If it moves and nothing in `serialize.c` or `sys_user.c` did, look at what was added. Making it independent of its process - a fixed GC pause and a forced collection before the loop - is a known improvement and is still not done. Then 1506.201 -> 897.665, -40.4%, and `serialize.c` was untouched again: the allocator underneath it stopped being a linear scan. That is the same sensitivity this note has always described, finally pointing at something worth fixing - the sentence above says to look at what was added, and the answer this time was that something was taken away. See `alloc_table`. **897.665 -> 771.350 (-14.1%), recorded on 2 October**: 823 -> 775 across 3b52773, the libc's memory functions a word at a time (`testing.md` 18.329), measured either side of it; the rest is the allocator's bins found by their bit (ecf6957, 18.307).
serialize.unit: counter ticks per operation, QEMU -icount shift=0
